title: Bhishma's vow
carry: a true reason, not the whole one

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhishma's vow began without Bhishma: a scent by the Yamuna, a fisherman's condition, and a king who said no and kept longing — the no and the longing, side by side. Who did you tell about a quiet no? Day seven hundred eleven.
screen: `THE NO AND THE LONGING, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Devavrata, the heir, has watched his father grow quiet and pale, sitting lost in thought, and he can't find a reason for it anywhere. The kingdom is at peace, and nothing is missing that he can see. So the son does something that takes a little nerve with a king. He stands before him and asks straight out: everything in the kingdom is going well, so why are you grieving? And Shantanu answers him. Just not completely.
screen: `WHY ARE YOU GRIEVING?` → `THE SON ASKS STRAIGHT OUT.` → `THE FATHER ANSWERS, PARTLY.`

segments.voice: Here is Shantanu's answer, in the text's sense. You are my only son. And the wise say that a man with one son is like a man with none. You're a warrior, always among weapons. If you fell in battle, what would become of our line? That's what troubles me. Every word of it is something the king could mean. In the world of the poem, a royal line resting on one young warrior is a real worry. But it isn't the reason he's grieving, and the text lets us see that. Shantanu is dressing a private longing in a public concern. He can't say, I want a woman whose father demands your crown. So he says, I'm afraid for the family. Devavrata hears it, and he doesn't argue. He thinks it over, and then he goes to someone who would know: an old minister, devoted to his father. He asks him what's really behind the king's grief. And the old man tells him: the fisherman's daughter by the Yamuna, and her father's condition, that her son must be king. Now Devavrata knows what his father couldn't say. And notice what he does not do. He doesn't confront his father with it. He doesn't sulk about a crown he might lose. He listens to the half answer, quietly finds the other half, and starts to think about what he can do. A true reason, not the whole one. The vow to come rests on a son who heard the difference.
screen: `ONE SON IS LIKE NO SON.` · `A LONGING DRESSED AS WORRY.` · `THE OLD MINISTER TELLS HIM.` · `HE DOESN'T CONFRONT HIS FATHER.` · then, large: `A TRUE REASON, NOT THE WHOLE ONE.`

segments.voice: Settle your feet on the floor and let the breath come in and go out. Bring to mind someone near you who seems a little off lately: a parent, a partner, a friend, a coworker. Maybe they've said they're fine. Don't try to solve them. Just hold them in mind with some curiosity. Breathe in, and wonder what they might not be able to say. Breathe out, and let your guesses go. Leave room for them to tell you, someday, in their own words. The bell holds the time.
Bhishma's vow. Before the vow, a son who hears his father's half answer, and goes to find the rest.
Your line: a true reason, not the whole one. Today, when someone says they're fine, ask one more gentle question. Day seven hundred eleven.

howItsDone: In some Hindu families, caring for aging parents and honoring their wishes is treated as a child's duty, and Bhishma's devotion to his father is held up in retellings as an example of it.

what it means: that worry was real, but it covered a longing he couldn't say aloud.
